chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Fazzal, from Dawud ibn Farqad, from Abu Yazeed al-Hammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent four angels for the destruction of the people of Lut: Jibra'il, Mikail, Israfil, and Karoubil. So they passed by Ibrahim (peace be upon him) while they were wearing turbans. They greeted him, but he did not recognize them. He saw their good physical build and said: 'None shall serve these except I myself,' and he was a man of hospitality.

So he roasted a fat calf for them until it was cooked, then he brought it near to them. When he placed it in front of them, he saw that their hands did not reach for it. He deemed them strange and conceived fear of them. When Jibra'il saw that, he removed the turban from his face, and Ibrahim recognized him. He said: 'You are he.' He said: 'Yes.'
And Sarah, his wife, passed by. They gave her the good news of Is'haq and after Is'haq of Yaqoub. She said: 'What did Allah, Mighty and Majestic, say?' So they answered her with what is in the Book.

So Ibrahim said to them: 'For what have you come?' They said: 'For the destruction of the people of Lut.' He said to them: 'If there are among them one hundred believers, would you destroy them?' Jibra'il said: 'No.' He said: 'If there are fifty?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'If there are thirty?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'If there are twenty?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'If there are ten?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'If there are five?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'If there is one?' He said: 'No.'
He said: 'Indeed, in it is Lut.' They said: 'We know better who is in it; we shall rescue him and his family, except for his wife; she shall be of those who remain behind.'
ai.seo_question: What was the condition for sparing the people of Lut from destruction according to the angels' conversation with Ibrahim?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi highlights the hospitality of Prophet Ibrahim (AS) and the specific role of the four archangels, including Karoubil, in the destruction of Sodom. It emphasizes the theological principle of divine mercy sparing a city for the sake of even a single righteous believer, a concept central to Shia exegesis regarding the preservation of the faithful amidst corruption. The dialogue underscores that while the majority might be destroyed, the presence of one true believer like Lut ensures the city's temporary reprieve.
